I wrote a funny story about modern relationships and the pandemic of ‘incompatibility.’ Here you go:

Non-Domestic Partnership
-----------------------------

She: I’m monogamous.
Him: I’m polyamorous.

She: I’m anxiously attached.
Him: I’m avoidantly attached.

She: I want to live in a nice suburb.
Him: I’ll die before I leave Brooklyn.

She: I squeeze toothpaste from the top.
Him: I squeeze it from the bottom, so that’s a dealbreaker.

She: I’m an atheist.
Him: I’m a pagan who worships Dionysus.

She: Shoes off in the house.
Him: I sleep in my sneakers. Just in case.

She: Top sheet is essential.
Him: Top sheets are a scam by Big Linen.

She: I don’t date under 5’11”
Him: I’m 5’8”. I’m wearing inserts.

She: I don’t date under 30.
Him: I’m 24.
She: Really?
Him: I don’t know whether to be flattered or insulted.

She: …
Him: …
She: Seems like we’re incompatible.
Him: Yes.

She: But you’re hot.
Him: You’re hot too.

She: And actually I love you.
Him: I love you too.

She: And yet we’re incompatible for domestic partnership.
Him: We’ll need to get creative.

And so the two began a non-domestic partnership. It started in their coworking space in Midtown at 2AM after even the cleaning lady went home to sleep. They stripped each other of all clothing and fogged the windows of one of the call booths. If it hadn’t been for his noise-cancelling headphones, the one remaining grindsetter sitting at a triple-monitor hot-desk might have heard muffled sounds like this:

She: FUCK!
Him: GOD!

Eventually it spread to the daytime when they went up to the rooftop in their winter jackets, hid behind the ventilation shaft, and cupped each other’s mouths so they could scream without the neighbors hearing them:

She: OOOOOF!
Him: YEAH JUST LIKE THAT!

They were not allowed into each other’s homes. That would start a domestic partnership and – as we’ve covered – they were incompatible. They would never meet one another’s families, or become one another’s emergency contacts, or share passwords to the same streaming services. They would never adopt a pet together. One would never take care of the other when they were sick. But the love was undeniable and so it spread.

She: I want more.
Him: I do too.
She: Let’s add the gym.
Him: Which one?
She: Vital.
Him: That’s a climbing gym
She: Yes.
Him: But I don’t climb.
She: They have solo bathrooms with benches and showers inside of them.
Him: I’ll get a membership.

And so their non-domestic partnership spread to the gym, and to all the other places of their lives untouched by the homemaking instinct. It did not spread to the supermarket, the DMV, or the doctor’s office. It definitely did not spread to IKEA. These were the domain of domestic partnerships. Instead, it spread to the nightclub, the coffee shop, and the rare books section of Strand. At these places they did things beyond merely undressing one another. They learned languages together. They explored the intricacies of one another’s pasts. They gave each other matching temporary tattoos. They listened to “their song.” (Uptown Funk by Bruno Mars.)

They were honest people, and so when they went on dates with serious prospects, they’d warn their dates that they were in a committed NDP.

Date: What’s an NDP?
She: A non-domestic partnership.
Date: Sorry, I’m looking for something more traditional.
She: So am I.

She became happily married. He entered a non-hierarchical polycule with an anchor partner, a nesting partner, and the nesting partner’s lesbian metamour. And yet the NDP became increasingly serious, filling up all the nondomestic cracks in their lives, edging out hobbies, TV shows, networking events, girls nights out, boys nights out, and book clubs. It grew to a crescendo:

She: I want kids.
Him: I also want kids.
She: I mean I want them with you.
Him: That sounds logistically difficult.
She: We’re creative people.
Him: OK let’s do it.

Their first-born was named James. He was emergency-delivered at 11PM in a hotel bar by a female business executive who claimed to be a doula.

She: Hold my hand.
Him: Is this really happening?
She: Oh god it’s coming.
Him: Are we really doing this right now?
She: Shut the fuck up and hold my hand!
Him: I see its head.
She: Nononono, I can’t, I can’t.
Him: Breathe!
She: RAAAAAHHHHHHH!
Him: It’s a boy!

Children tend to accept their immediate surroundings, and so James and, later, his sister Emily didn’t question why they were raised between movie theatre matinees, 24-hour diners, and the Rose Reading Room at the New York Public Library. That changed when James entered grade school, which he attended through Zoom on his mom’s laptop (at the coworking space where he was conceived). James started to have questions:

James: Mommy?
She: Mhm.
James: Why don’t me and Emily have a home?
She: Your father and I are in a nondomestic partnership.
James: What’s that?
She: It’s a type of modern relationship that acknowledges the freedom and sovereignty of both individuals. 
James: But the other kids in my school have homes.
She: Their parents are not in modern relationships.
James: But dad told me that you have a husband with kids and that you all live in a home.
She: That’s true. It’s not a very modern relationship.
James: Is it better to be in a modern relationship?
She: I don’t know.

James grew up and applied to the most stable jobs he could find: accountant, actuary, compliance officer, residential real estate agent. He ended up as a social security eligibility specialist. Despite this, he continued to live across the spaces that felt most like home: the Walgreens on 34th St, the Port Authority Bus Terminal, and a high-end bath-house in the Flatiron District called Othership. The owner let him sleep on the cedar planks of the saunas and even played him mysterious flute music to help him drift off to sleep.

Meanwhile, James’s mother moved to the suburbs of Hudson where she and her domestic family enjoyed shopping at boutiques of Main Street and attending revolutionary war reenactments on weekends. She visited James whenever her advertising job brought her into Manhattan. 

James’s father moved into a large Victorian in Ditmas Park with his non-hierarchical polycule, which had grown to over 100 members. Since domestic life kept his him busy, James was forced to commute to Brooklyn to see his father. They ate momos at a Tibetan restaurant near the Q train every other Tuesday.

At 42, James felt stuck at his job and entered a mid-life crisis. Soon after, his mother died. Neither he nor his father nor his estranged sister Emily were invited to the funeral. None of them made it into the will. That was the agreement that his father and mother had set back in the year 2026, when nondomestic partnerships first became popular. 

And so, three nights after the funeral, James and his father snuck into the home of his mother’s domestic family. They broke open a window with a rock from the garden that her husband tended. Once inside, they stole the urn of her ashes from the fireplace mantel, their barbarian silhouettes casting shadows by the light of the still-burning fire. Their shadows stretched across the living room carpet, and the sofa, and the domestic husband who stood behind the sofa slack-jawed:

Husband: What are you doing?
Him: Freeing her!
Husband: Stop that! She’s mine!
James: Love belongs to no one!—
—James surprised himself by shouting.

The husband chased them from the property with a shotgun – that’s how domestic this family had become. They escaped the jaws of the family dog just in time by hopping the electric fence, accepting the shock that shot through their bodies. In fact, they needed it as raw energy for the coming sprint across the open fields.

Out of the corner of his eye, the father saw other forms racing toward them. It was his non-hierarchical polycule, here to assert hierarchy over his one wild and precious life. They rushed forth through the tall grass, screaming like banshees.

James: Dad, they’re gaining on us!
Him: Run for the treeline!

They dodged between the trunks and boulders, eventually losing the polycule amongst a dense expanse of brambles. At last, they found a rushing river that James’s mother would have loved. It seemed to babble in her native tongue, and it carried along dead leaves and stray branches. James broke the urn over a stone. Its porcelain shards scattered between the pebbles of the shore. They each grabbed a fistful of ash and prepared to throw it into the river.

James: I never learnt her name.
Him: I didn’t either.
James: Shouldn’t we say something?
Him: She hated words.
James: Still…
Him: OK.

He cleared his throat:

I crave your breasts, your neck, your hands. 
I whisper feral prayers to your giggling flesh, like a
leopard prowling the streets of Manhattan,
hunting, sniffing, feasting until my belly bursts.

The holy men wrote “thy love was better than wine.”
Unseal the cask again and let me
drown in waves of your ecstasy. Upon my death,
let seas of luminous juice drown over heaven.

I eat your memory. I drink your memory.
It fills me. It heats me from within,
makes my spine prickle and spark, a column of 
flame that burns me into new shapes from the inside-out.

If anyone asks how you became the earth, don’t
explain the miracle.
Just kiss me on the lips.
Like this.

When someone asks what it means to “kill for love,” don’t
get into theology. Simply say, 
“This meat was made from living things,” and,
“These grapes were plucked from the living vine.”

And death, I feel, is very near.

Most therapists have struck me as mildly sucky. So back when I was depressed, I used a brief period of lucidity to construct a hardcore process for finding a great one. Here is my Hardcore Therapist Finding Process:

1. Modalities: I researched which therapy modalities might be helpful. (Eg Existential? Cognitive behavioral? Etc. These days you can describe your problem to an LLM and get some recs)

2. Big list: I went into the Psychology Today database of therapists, filtered by therapy modality, and quickly made a list of ~30-50 therapists who maybe had a good vibe

3. Vibe check: Went to their personal websites and engaged any media I could find from them online for addtl vibe check. Narrowed down to top 10

4. Initial consultation: Emailed the 10 asking for a free 10-15min discovery call to see if we’re a fit. After the call, asked myself questions like: How comfortable did I feel? Are they a dummy? Is my intuition a yes?

5. First meetings: I took first meetings with about 5 and did a richer vibe check. This narrowed it down to the therapist I eventually chose, who was excellent and still one of my favorite people!

When you find a great therapist, this becomes a public service for your network, because then you can refer your friends to them. (The therapist I found is still working with one of my best friends)

It seems like if you want your religion to maintain long-term integrity, it helps to embed its principles in something akin to a simple mental executable file, like a .dmg or .exe

I’m learning how even *early* Christianity featured many different sects, each with dramatically different interpretations of Jesus’s teachings. This makes sense to me bc the guy taught in parables that confused even the 12 original apostles

There’s evidence of similar interpretational drift around Christianity’s foremost theologian & organizer, Paul

I compare this to Buddhism, the ~whole of which you can extrapolate (through practice & integrated insight) from the four noble truths. I believe it’s possible to self-discover many other features of the religion if you contemplated these four sentences alone in a cave. They’re a mental installer file

Certainly there are lots of different and weird versions of Buddhism, but I’m astounded by the way the three major yanas in Buddhism feel like the result of *building* on one another’s foundations rather than the result of *schisms* from radically different interpretations

(Although a simple google search does reveal big schisms in Buddhism I wasn’t aware of. So take the thing above with a grain of salt, but I do think there’s something to it)

Believers often see Jesus's documented miracles as the prime evidence of his divinity. But I'm learning that in Jesus's era, it was quite common to mythologize venerated individuals, attributing miracles to them - eg:

Divine conception: Alexander was conceived by Zeus. Augustus & Plato by Apollo

Miraculous attributes: Pythagoras had a golden thigh, could appear in multiple places at once & many other abilities

Jewish holy men: Hanina ben Dosa was a Jewish contemporary of Jesus who also lived in lower Galilee (within <1day walking distance in fact). He could heal at a distance, banish demons, prompt vinegar to burn like oil (for a lamp), and turn on and off the rain

(Hanina ben Dosa was just one of several Jewish charismatics living in the region during the period: healers, exorcists, prophetic leaders, etc)

This can be narrated a few ways:
A. Only the miracles of Jesus were real*; the others were fake (this would preserve the uniqueness of Jesus's divine status)
B. All the miracles of the time were real. We've either forgotten how to perform them or somehow the conditions for miracles no longer exist
C. None of the miracles of the time were real. Historical ppl were gullible, hallucinating a lot, and/or had some different relationship to the concept of miracles that moderns struggle to fathom

* definition of "real" here = something like "physical reality was altered by divine agency"

Personally, I put ~5-10% probability on B & the rest on C. (Although I'll clarify that I also believe in the exciting possibility that some apparent "miracles" were actually advanced psychosomatic techniques – I've witnessed some of these) 

I suspect that many Christians would want to deny the ideas that either Jesus was not uniquely miraculous (B) or that miracles did not exist (C)

I'll end this post with a few quotes from Jesus that feel relevant here:

Matthew 12:38-39
Pharisees: "Teacher, we want to see a sign from you."
Jesus: "A wicked and adulterous generation asks for a sign!" (this line is repeated later in Matthew)

Luke 23:8-9
Herod wants to see Jesus "perform a sign of some sort." Jesus declines.

John 4:48
"'Unless you people see signs and wonders...you will never believe."

I can almost imagine Jesus showing up again and saying to us, "O ye of little faith. I showed you the way to create heaven on earth and you demand miracles for proof"

This sounds crazy to say, but I regularly feel grateful for the period of severe depression I had from ~2018-2020

At that time, I had been pushing myself into a life that was terrible for me, like a person smashing themselves into a wall

My Self had tried to warn me of this for years by sending me a sense *wrongness*. "Don't smash yourself into that wall." I ignored it and kept smashing myself into the wall

In response, my Self sent an even greater sense of wrongness that began to exhaust me. So I sought out ways to overcome the exhaustion: not just with things like coffee & modafinil, but also with "healthy habits" like exercise, dance, diet, meditation, therapy, good sleep, etc. These things *did* rejuvenate me...filling me with energy to smash myself against the wall again

Finally, my Self simply immobilized me. For well over a year, I could barely get myself off of a mattress. Now, not only could I not smash myself against a wall, I could barely even summon the energy to get up and pee. I would lie there for hours until some distant voice would urge "You have to get up now, or your bladder will literally burst"

At the time, I thought that my only source of value = my ability to contribute. So this state of immobility felt like a fate worse than death, as I became an active burden on those around me. I wanted to kms

I've since seen that this desire to kms was actually a form of love in disguise. Truly: it was a desire for the self-harming version of myself to die. And then eventually, painfully, it did

Importantly, I will say that some forms of depression *really can* be alleviated through healthier habits like diet, exercise, and socializing. But, in some cases, these healthy habits will only give a person more energy to throw themselves back into an unhealthy job, relationship, social circle, etc

So, for these types of depressed ppl, please don't get angry at them for "not wanting to get better." They might just be protecting themselves from a false rejuvenation, one that would only give them energy to smash themselves into a wall again

There's a different way to help them if you can access a spacious vibe. You can help them come to their own (unforced) realization – a realization of why their Self, out of love, has decided to immobilize them

I can say that, personally, I absolutely needed to be immobilized as a step toward the incredible life I have today

I would lie there for hours until some distant voice would urge "You have to get up now, or your bladder will literally burst"

Some of my friends are confused at why I’m suddenly interested in religion. I already have my own thing going on with god/awareness/whatever-you-want-to-call-it and it’s good stuff. What’s the point of religion then?

Well, solo worship is different than collective reverence & practice *with others.* And for that, it’s helpful to have a shared framework or mythos

I’ve tried running containers where there’s one Daoist, one Buddhist, one Christian mystic, one New Ager, etc, and we practice techniques from the different traditions. Socially speaking, these containers were beautiful. But in terms of collective mystic experience, it was a bit weaksauce. I think focusing on just one tradition brings more depth & specificity than gathering people just on the basis of “spirituality” 

By analogy, imagine you gather lovers of “fantasy” (as an analogy to gathering lovers of “god”). Doug is into epic fantasy, Stacy like historical romantasy, and Raven enjoys young adult urban fairty tales. “I love fantasy,” says Doug. “Agreed, fantasy so inspiring,” says Stacy. “And magic is totally cool,” says Raven. But unfortunately, the conversation peters out. There are only so many words you can use to express love of “fantasy” in general when you don’t have shared referents

Now imagine you gather Tolkien fans in particular. They’re going to spend hours intensely channeling their love of fantasy through interacting over specific characters, scenes, and worldbuilding elements. Just as creativity needs constraints, shared love needs specificity, and shared religious practice benefits from the specificity of a particular religion’s metaphysics, gods, techniques, etc. 

Like metaphors, religions are what turn the ineffable into poetry that we can share

What's your religious history? Here is mine:

Born to an ethnically Jewish dad, Catholic mom, neither practicing. I wasn’t brought up with religious beliefs, but we still celebrated Hanukkah, Christmas, etc. (It took until my 30s to realize how spiritually lit my parents actually are) 

⁠At ~17, I decided I was an atheist & materialist

At ~18, I got into breath and body-scan meditation (no tradition) and occasionally experienced ~mystical states. At the time, I didn’t really narrate them into a spirituality. It was more like “wow it’s so cool what the brain can do!”

Later, in my 20s. experienced all sorts of crazy things: Eg witnessed hard-to-dispute evidence for what ppl call “energy healing.” Went on a silent Rinzai Zen retreat and experienced something that resonates with what some Buddhists call “stream entry” (maybe?)

Started searching for a spiritual tradition I could jive with, since Zen felt too renunciative/stark. Discovered Vajrayana Buddhism by running into an image of Vajrakilaya with no small amount of shock. Unlike most Buddhism in the West, Vajrayana harnesses body, mind, and relationships as vehicles for awakening rather than obstacles to it

Vajrayana is still feels GOATed to me. I find its aesthetics, techniques, and views so beautiful and so psychotechnologically advanced that it almost feels like a gift from aliens. But I’ve concluded that most Westerners will simply never have the cultural & lineage-access to do Vajrayana the way Tibetans do it. I do think the principles can be very carefully adapted to our cultural context. But in the meantime, it feels inauthentic to me to LARP as a Tibetan. 

This got me reflecting whether there was a way for me to practice a spiritual system that I have more grounding in as a Westerner. And the good news is that (IMO) you can practice almost any other spiritual tradition in a kind of Vajrayana-based way (with insight into "emptiness" as the base)

I heard that some Tibetans talk about “Jesus dharma,” and started looking into that as a possibility. Meanwhile, I’ve met a number of friends who I regard as Christian mystics (@feral_eyes, @kailajlim) and I was impressed by how brightly their hearts shine. So lately I’ve been doing a fair amount of prayer, going to various churches, and engaging in obsessive Bible study as a way to connect with Christianity. My hope is that I might find/create a local NYC group of mystical or post-Christians to practice with

"Share your happiness with the world." Duh, right? That's some basic b***h stuff. But recently a Buddhist nun said this to me in this sort of knowing way and it's been changing my life

I realized that I am often not only hiding my happiness but actively turning it down. I'm doing this to fit in, to connect with the zeitgeist. And today's zeitgeist has made it borderline offensive to be happy

"You're happy? What about the war? And misaligned AI? And Tr*mp???"

Being happy is uncool right now in academia, amongst liberals, amongst humanitarians, and in art circles. It's cringe in many locales of NYC and twitter. So I noticed that when I walk smiling through the streets, I start to feel like I'm Out Of Touch

This nun, however, was pointing out that if you don't share your happiness, if you don't let thy cup runneth over, you're depriving other people of something that can light them up

No one wants to be seen as naive, spiritually bypassing, or brushing aside the horrors of the world. But a mature form of happiness, one that acknowledges these horrors, and which shines despite them...? that strikes me as exactly the sort of thing we need right now

I hurt myself w meditation for 10 years. The problem was not the techniques, but my intent behind them

I recently got honest with myself about *why* I was meditating. The answer was something like "to gain increasing control over my mind until I become perfect." Oops! 

How did that happen? 

When I first started meditating around 2009, my intent was explorative. I was like "meditating huh? sounds interesting. I'll mess around with that." It was an autotelic activity – one done for its own sake. And you know what? I still regularly entered states that Serious Meditators call "attainments." 

My reaction to these states wasn't "Yes! I have attained the attainment!" Instead it was texting my then-girlfriend stuff like "Holy crap meditation feels amazing!"

Soon enough, however, I started bringing a different intention to meditation. It changed from an autotelic activity (done for its own sake) to an *instrumental* one (done for some other purpose)

That purpose was what Buddhists call "bodhicitta" – to awaken for the sake of all beings. My motivation to meditate now came from a more solemn and controlling place. Meditation was not for fun! It was an Important Duty! Serious Business. If my sit "went poorly" then this was Morally Bad, because I would be worse at Helping All Beings

Don't get me wrong, I think bodhicitta is a beautiful intention that can come from a light, playful place of "chanda," which I unpack in the quote tweet. But that's not how I went about it

Ironically I went about it from a place of "tanha" – the craving that Buddhist meditation is supposed to relieve. I was craving perfection: for both me and for the world. As a result, my meditation sits often *increased* my suffering, as I tried to tame my unruly mind into better behavior

I am now interested in returning to meditation as an activity that I do for it's own sake. I want to savor meditation for the same way I savor movies, sex, dance, gift-making, amazing meals, and hanging out w babies & animals. I want to savor it as a form of connection, or as a form of play

I have some unusual habits that I think others might benefit from. Here are 3:

1. Work in museums
Every so often I spend my workday at the Metropolitan Museum of Art or the natural history museum. I find the spacious environments relaxing. In most museums there are cafes are nooks that are great for laptop work. When I need a break, I go around and get filled with inspired by the collection

2. Babysit every week
Babysitting my goddaughter is typically the highlight of my week. If you have a friend with kids, you can try proactively offering to babysit regularly to give them alone time or a date night. You'll be doing yourself just as much of a service by spending time with a little squirt that brings out your playful side and helps you stop fretting about the meaning of life for a bit

3. Buddies for everything
Solo discipline is hard and often not worth it. So instead I bring on accountability buddies for everything. When I wanted to develop a meditation habit, I started to sit with my friend Ren across the street every morning at 8:45am. When I wanted to make progress on my novel, I created a writers group. When I had a bunch of tasks I was avoiding, I created this now-famous forcing party: https://t.co/p5GwU5eEVY

If you struggle to meet people romantically, it might be because you don’t play your role

In traditional courtship, the roles are:
• The woman signals availability through the way she holds herself
• The man responds by approaching

Gender norms have opened, so now anyone can play either role in rooms where ppl are more alternative

There’s also the third gender-fluid option where both people do availability and approach, like when you gradually find your way closer to one another on a dance floor, responding to one another’s subtle cues

It’s obvious how to play the approach role. The basics are that you just go up to someone and say hey

The availability role is more subtle. We often talk about external signs of availability: dressing in ways that say “come flirt with me,” flirty body language, etc. However, really availability is more of an internal stance. It’s a vibe that says “If you think you’re a match, come talk to me”

For instance, I know gorgeous women who dress beautifully that no one ever approaches because they put out the vibe of unavailability with their entire being

I've been engaging "god" a lot more. Get ready for an obscure tweet

Why use this word, "god?" First of all, it's just a word that I grew up with that automatically invokes reverence, benevolence, and awe

But also, simply calling it "awareness," "presence," or "the dao" misses that it seems to have certain agent-like qualities. These include an affinity for and invitation toward certain ways of relating to the world

The danger – which we see in many participants in Judeochristian religions – is to model god too closely on a human. Then we start attributing more anthropomorphic qualities like judgment and active intervention in affairs

As far as I can tell, god does not judge, at least not in any sort of way similar to human morality. God's negative judgement inheres in immoral behavior itself: bad behavior feels bad. (If you're paying attention.) The punishment for immoral behavior isn't a lightning bolt or being sent to hell after you die. It's that you've just hurt yourself, buddy. Now you'll need to invest time healing or undoing the damage if you want to feel better

As far as I can tell, god does not actively intervene in affairs. God influence seems to be more like a flower's fragrance; alluring us rather than controlling us. It is most influential when we ourselves choose to breathe it in

This influence can be viewed two ways:

Through the objective/materialist lens, god's influence seems to be toward a certain type of skillful integration or "concrescence." This is a fancy word meaning "the coalescence or growing together of parts originally separate." (I also suggest the word "polyphony" here. Polyphony speaks to a manner of integration that preserves the unique virtues of the things being integrated. I contrast it to the word "merging.") God's influence is like a magnet or a gravity well in that it can still be resisted through force, even as the influence inheres in that being that exerts the force

Through the subjective/experience lens, the process above has a certain feeling to it when one is participating in it (by choice or accident). It feels like grace, flow, opening, beauty, attraction/eros, and love. These are the phenomenological markers of processes that facilitate concrescence

The classic forces of community-formation are losing their hold in 1st-world democracies:
religion
ethnicity
neighborhoods
professional associations/unions
civic society (elks, masons, etc)
oppressed demographic
extended family
nationalism
gender

The remaining binding forces include:
workplace
subculture
ideology

However, the strength of these remaining binding forces is pretty weak. For most workplaces, subcultures, and ideologies, your "community" is not going to have your back when times get hard

This might paint a pessimistic picture. But there is actually one strong binding force which remains: friendship!

Friendship – possibly due to its illegibility and informality – has tended to take a backseat to other binding forces throughout much of history. (With notable exceptions – eg sworn friendships in medieval Europe and Imperial China.)

However, now that the other binding forces are disintegrating, friendship has the chance to emerge from the cracks in society

I suspect that the massive trend in preferences for love-marriages vs instrumental-marriages demonstrates a bigger movement in society. We now want to be drawn together by inherent chemistry instead of more formal forces like family ties, ethnicity, or economic advantage

Previous forces of community-formation were typically supported by more formal structures: clubhouses, holidays, rites. The competition of other binding forces has diminished, so now structures are emerging for friendship: Friendsgiving, group chats, coliving houses, "chosen family" commitments, group vacations

Fractal – the thing I'm working on – is one attempt to build communities from friendship networks by experimenting with structures like these (and more)

It may seem like a dark moment in history, where all the forces that bound us obligatorily together are falling apart. But imagine this: maybe, for the first time, we actually get to *choose* one another. And now we're learning how:

In his classic Bowling Alone, Robert Putnam defined two types of social capital: bonding and bridging.

Bonding social capital connects people within a group—eg family, close friends, religious or cultural communities.

Bridging social capital connects people across groups—eg coworkers, acquaintances, or interfaith alliances.

His metaphor is that bonding SC is superglue while bridging SC is WD-40.

Hot take I’ve been chewing on:
Part of the breakdown of social fabric in the West partly stems from liberal ideologies that pushed against bonding social capital. They did this often for good reason. Bonding SC historically created strong ingroup cohesion but also a lot of coercion through ossified norms + sharp outgroup animosity – eg prejudice, and even violence in the case of blacks, gays, etc.

The move toward a less coercive and violent world required a lot of bonding SC to be weakened or broken. And that breaking worked in some ways: it expanded individual freedom, challenged oppressive systems, and opened up space for bridging across tribes.

But now we’re seeing the side effects: loneliness, fragmentation, meaning crises, a sense that no one truly belongs anywhere.

So the modern social design challenge is to recreate bonding SC without the standard failure modes. Strong ingroups but with (a) greater tolerance toward innocuous norm-deviation and also (b) generosity toward broader society

My new crackpot theory of what makes for Great Art is that Great Art anneals the "emotion body" toward greater accuracy and/or possibility

Examples: 

Epics
The novel Dune, Malick's film Tree of Life, and Vivaldi's Four Seasons remap the emotion body toward the greater scale of civilization, god's grace, and seasonality, respectively. The audience feels *moved* (which is the typical experience of annealing). Why? Because this is a move toward accuracy. They'd forgotten the ways in which they are in fact continuous with vast transpersonal phenomena. Key phenomenology: awe, rapture, reverence, sublimity

Intimate dramas
Anna Karenina, the film Boyhood, or the songs of Billie Holiday induce the emotion body to re-include parts of ourselves that we forgot or repressed – eg our foibles, our childhood self, and the heartbreaks we've suffered. This is also a move toward accuracy. It's like feeling your own organs. Key phenomenology: sorrow, tenderness, longing, levity

Possibility expanders
Everything Everywhere All At Once, great surrealists like Dalí, and the Beatles' "I Am the Walrus" induce us to map ourselves onto subjects or things that cause a sort of emotion body dysmorphia. Art in this category reminds us that we are not fixed – our boundaries and possible instantiations are fluid. Key phenomenology: playfulness, liberation, disorientation/existential vertigo

Notes:
• Great Art also often introduces Big Ideas (eg the Foundation series). But if art tries to do so without the annealing component – in which the audience feels "moved" – the Big Ideas fall flat
• What do I mean by the "emotion body"? Something like: the aspects of ourselves that are currently available to be felt
• I almost wrote "energy body" instead of "emotion body," but the world is not ready for that kind of language

There's an alternative to cutting off bad relationships. You can use the new context effect: choose to spend time ONLY in contexts that bring out good behavior (or at least *new* behavior)

The problem: default contexts can get diseased. You might think you can change them from within, but in practice this can be intractable – there's too much ill-will and history built up *inside* the context

Eg. maybe you & you dad always get in fights when u come home for dinner. But maybe the dynamic is different when:
• You bring a friend/partner to dinner
• You go hiking instead
• You do an activity like boardgames or target-shooting where the focus is on some external activity instead of directly on one another

Ever had the experience of seeing someone from work or an old friend in a totally different context. It's like meeting them anew? The new context tactic has this effect

You might face some stubbornness from the other person when you propose the new context. We feel safe in what's familiar, even if it's bad for us. So you might have to be firm: "I want to interact in this new way. The alternative for me is to not interact"

The new @slatestarcodex post on priesthoods illustrates why it’s often much easier to do useful (or even groundbreaking) work in a field than you’d think

Wherever there’s a developed field, you can bet that the field has a “priesthood” – experts who have their own status hierarchies 

Priesthoods often initially ensure that status is awarded to work that meets a certain bar of quality. However, over time, they pretty reliably either 
(a) drift to a wack/false standard of quality (eg academic architecture) or 
(b) fossilize around an initial standard that fails to update itself. 
At this point, they’ll often start discouraging genuinely good work

You can identify whether a field has a decayed standard. (Which, mind you, requires deep engagement with the priesthood, not ignoring it.) If the standard is decayed, then the ground is fertile for some up-and-comer to pioneer actually-good work

This person will often face the poo-pooing of the priesthood. There are standard ways to deal with this:
• Have your work actually be good despite the priesthood’s poo-pooing (duh. But smart ppl want this to be enough on its own; it usually isn’t. You also need things like:)
• Ally with heterodox-yet-respected members of the priesthood
• Be better at engaging the public (though catering to the public comes with its own set of traps)
• Start your own institutions with alternate sources of status and funding

When you zoom out, the evolutionary function is actually quite beautiful. Priesthoods are good at creating the illusion of being eternal. However, the historical move to greater and greater quality looks like priesthoods arising to maintain standards, then falling away to be replaced by new ones, like a phoenix combusting to arise again and again

Warning: minor spoilers of action movies

TENSION
----------
a. High stakes (duh)
- Classic ones are world, city, or character lives at stake

- Dark Night: scene of Joker on foot vs obviously more powerful batcycle

c. Uncertainty ("What's happening?/What's next?")
- Children of Men: protag car gets away from mob as police cars go toward mob...is mob coming back? Are the police going to chase the protags?

d. Desperation
- GoT: Battle of the Bast*rds...Bolton's army closing in on Rob

DEMONSTRATIONS OF ABILITY/VIRTUE
------------------------------------------
e. Clever use of environment or gadget
- Dark Knight: Joker's people down the police copter with just wires strung between buildings
- Gladiator: "Work together!" arena scene where Maximus's gladiators the enemies' chariots and weapons against them

f. Heroes or villains demonstrating badassery
- Matrix: Trinity runs up wall and does crazy kick
- Ground pound moments: the many scenes where a hero/villain is against the ropes and then finds their "true strength" and, eg, go on a punching rampage
- Especially when secret abilities unveiled - "Woah, Batman’s car has that ability?"
- Object of power returned to hero/villain, eg LoTR: Staff returned to Gandalf

HEROISM
----------
g. Sacrifices
- Especially when character redeems themselves through sacrifice, eg LoTR: Boromir

h. Saves
- LoTR: The eagles rescue our protags

i. Teamwork 
- Avengers: Ultron: epic collaboration between the powers of the Avengers as they storm a base
- We esp. like teamwork when it emerges amongst rival sides. Thor: Ragnarok: Thor teams up with Loki to stop Hela from destroying Asgard

SPECTACLE
------------
j. Iconic visuals
- Dark Knight: The truck flip moment, or when Batman's cycle bursts out of a mall and the wheels turn sideways
- Memorable details like in GoT: the sons of the harpy masks

k. Unique deaths
- Gladiator: That enemy gladiator lady in gold who is cut in half by the chariot blades
- Kill Bill vol. 2: Bill's death

l. Great choreography
- All Matrix films

m. Eye-popping environment
- Matrix: Reloaded: fighting on the steps of ornate mansion
- spiderman far from home: tower bridge scene
- Kong on Empire State Building

n. Unusual constraints
- Old Boy: stuck to just one hallway
- Dune: Paul knifefights Jamis but is stuck with shield-fighting instincts
- Inception: Joseph Gorden-Levitt has to fight in a rotating hallway

SURPRISES
------------
n. Sudden chaos
- Edge of Tomorrow: Tom Cruise’s carrier falls apart
- The Departed: ______ is suddenly shot

Advice I would give to a college freshman: 
These next four years, one of your main goals should be to figure out how not to have the rest of your life be a long series of soul-sapping jobs

If you want to be happy after college, learn how to do one or multiple of these:
• Run your own business doing something you love (eg massage, coaching, art direction, filmmaking etc)
• Become economically independent somehow (eg through 4hr Work Week-style automated businesses)
• Get really good at cold-reading potential bosses, colleagues, and team culture so you only choose to work in life-giving teams
• Go into business with friends
• Only work at places doing stuff you regard as meaningful. If you go for a period not being able to find one of these, *do not compromise.* Just be poor and/or go on govt aid with free govt health insurance

But most of all, just start building a big network of people who are pursuing the routes above and are happy with their work. Begin the habit of relying on them to find jobs/gigs by writing up blurbs saying [what you are looking for] and passing it around on social media, telling them in person, etc. 

You can start testing all these paths NOW, in college, through internships, or shadowing, or otherwise. Test them, especially during summer break! See what works for you!

A lot of your collegiate peers are heading for a hell-realm of flourescently lit offices where it's hard to connect with the meaning of work, most coworkers are numbed out, and free hours after work are spent too exhausted to do anything of consequence. Do not follow them into this hell-realm. Do not go gentle into that good night!!!

It’s crazy to me that our cultural desiderata for a marriage so wildly diverges from the realities of what I see

Ppl are looking to fall madly in love and then “keep the flame alive” for a lifetime. But if “keeping the flame alive” means staying madly in love & having regular amazing sex, well…maybe only 1 out of 1000 couples are like that

And so, in year ~five when sex is only happening once every few weeks (if at all), and the couple is essentially platonic, ppl feel like they’re failing, and might even get divorced

Guys…what if it turns out that we’re ~not biologically built for this fantasy marriage scenario we all seek? What if the volatile force of romance is just one means of bonding us deeply together so that then we can form lifelong partnerships from a different form of love, one that’s better suited for creating a stable environment for children? Platonic love

Moreover, why are we suffering from this cultural mass delusion, where we insist that marriages should not become ~platonic? 

I suspect it’s because of our atomization. Imagine you live in a suburb with two kids. Your family & friends live far away. The time-honored tradition of having mistresses and misters – previously a means for monogamous couples to stay married – is deemed unacceptable by the current culture waters. Work connections are superficial or fleeting (as workplaces these days have higher turnover). You have to depend on your spouse as the only relationship capable of imbuing you with liveliness

IMO the antidote is to 
(a) prioritize live within walking distance of ppl you love to put less pressure on marriage
(b) not only accept the default that long term partners become platonic, but look forward to it: platonic love is not a lesser form of love. Learn its intricacies and secrets

One of my roles/purposes in life is to act like a "superconnector" (ugh feels bad to use that word unironically 😬) Sometimes ppl ask me what this is like, so here is a post on that topic

I started life as a socially awkward nerd who had a hard time making more than 1 friend at a time. Then, at age...14 maybe?...I very abruptly adopted a new personality. Or more like "discovered" it, since it emerged fully fledged. The event was this: I met two hot girls at the mall who were from a different school...so they didn't realize I was a "loser." I wanted to impress them, so, BOOM new charismatic personality. Where did it come from? idk probably watching movies + being a camp counselor + staring like a lemur at the popular kids who shunned me

From that day, I started being a *lot* more social. It was exhausting, even though it turned out that I love people. I became interested in lots of different types. And I learned that I had a strange obsession with introducing types of people who don't normally interact. To this day, at 33, I still get enormous enjoyment from, say, introducing a libertarian SF tech bro to a queer Barcelonian artist and watching them find value in one another.

These days I pretty much treat this type of thing as a job, or like, my contribution to the human project. I like to facilitate these sort of collisions not just with people, but also with ideas or domains. Right now some of the most sophisticated psychologists (other than therapists) are people who manage people, woo masters, salespeople.

However these experts often lack the good parts of scientific epistemology, so their observations/theories r high variance.

Thus an IRL useful psychological research program would still import many scientific norms that enhance observational epistemology: mutual critique, checks against confirmation bias, awareness of selection effects, etc.
